tytul: The Loop That Feels Like Problem-Solving: How to Stop Overthinking
tresc_html:
When did you last replay a conversation that ended hours ago? And how many versions of your reply have you written since?

Maybe it was a message that just said "ok". You've now spent longer analyzing those two letters than the whole conversation lasted. Or a restaurant choice that needed three tabs of reviews, a close reading of two menus and a consultation with a friend. By this evening you'll have acted out the follow-up conversation in the shower three times, with three different endings, and lost the argument in two of them.

It feels like working on the problem. Most of the time, it's walking in circles around it.

Why does your brain keep doing this?

Overthinking is usually an attempt to get some control back. Your brain treats uncertainty as a problem to be solved, and it keeps promising that one more lap will finally produce the answer. It's a GPS saying "recalculating" over and over while you're sitting in a parking lot, working very hard and going nowhere.

Psychologists have a name for the stickiest version. Rumination is repetitive, passive thinking about how you feel, why you feel that way and what it might mean, without moving on to doing anything about it. It circles the same questions again and again, and each lap tends to leave you feeling worse rather than clearer.

Disclaimer: thinking things through is not the problem. Thinking them through for the fourteenth time is.

This loop works nights as well, and the night shift of the same loop has its own tricks. Here we're staying with the daytime version, the one that follows you to your desk.

Signs you're overthinking, not problem-solving:

  • The question in your head starts with "why" and never seems to end.
  • Each new lap brings no new information, just the same facts in a different order.
  • The longer you think, the worse you feel, instead of clearer.
  • You're looking for a certainty the situation can't give you.
  • You put off the decision "until you're sure", and sure never arrives.

Sometimes it starts early. The loop that starts before you get out of bed has its own biology, and it's worth knowing about if your overthinking tends to arrive with the alarm.

What research turned up:

In 2008, Susan Nolen-Hoeksema, Blair Wisco and Sonja Lyubomirsky pulled together years of work on rumination in Perspectives on Psychological Science. The picture was consistent: rumination deepens negative thinking, gets in the way of solving problems and makes it harder to act on the plans you do make. People often feel as if they're working things out while it happens. Feeling like you're working on it isn't proof that you are.

So what's the alternative, if "just stop thinking" doesn't work? In 2005, Ed Watkins and Michelle Moulds ran an experiment published in Emotion. People with depression were randomly asked to think about their problems in one of two ways. The abstract way focused on why: what the problem means, why it happened. The concrete way focused on how: what exactly happened and how it unfolded, moment by moment. Both lowered mood. The concrete group, though, came up with better solutions to social problems afterward.

Why keeps the loop open. How starts closing it. One limit to remember: the study involved people with depression, so it isn't a test on the general population, even though the idea has since been studied more widely.

Then, in 2014, Ethan Kross and colleagues published seven studies with 585 participants in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology. When people reflected on a stressful situation using their own name or "you" instead of "I", they got more distance from it. Before giving a speech or making a first impression, they felt less distressed, performed better in the eyes of observers and spent less time going over it afterward.

A small change in language makes room between you and the loop. It's a tool for distance, not a cure for anything, and the studies used short lab tasks rather than months of real life.

How to stop overthinking without trying to stop thinking:

  1. Swap "why" for "what next". When you notice the loop, ask a different question: "What's one thing I can do about this before tonight?" If the answer is "nothing", that's useful too. It means the thinking can stop for today.
  2. Talk to yourself by name for one minute. "Okay, Sam, what do you actually know here?" It sounds like something athletes do in shoe commercials, and honestly, it kind of is. It also buys you some of the distance the Kross studies measured.
  3. Get it out of your head and into words. Say the whole loop out loud in sixty seconds, then read back what you said. Loops sound very convincing inside your head and a lot shorter as text. If you're not sure whether to write it or say it, pick whichever you'll actually do.
  4. Set a stopping point for decisions with no perfect answer. Pick "good enough" and a date by which you'll decide. The restaurant menu is not a character test, and neither are most of the choices we treat like one.
  5. Name the feeling under the loop. Overthinking often sits on top of something simpler, like being afraid of getting it wrong or of being judged. Finding the feeling under the loop usually quiets the thinking more than another round of analysis.
[FEATURE: voice-notes | Sixty seconds out loud, then the loop is sitting there as text, which is usually shorter and less convincing than it sounded in your head.]

If the loop is taking your days, your sleep or your appetite, it's worth talking to a therapist about. You don't have to untangle it alone, and it helps to take the loop into your next session with a couple of concrete examples.

You can't think your way out of a loop that thinking built.

This is what MindSync's Between-session voice notes are for. Log the loop in sixty seconds, the question you keep asking, and the one next step you picked instead. Give it time, and your Weekly & monthly summaries turn those entries into something you can read: which questions keep coming back, week after week. Then pin the one that won't let go in your Workspace and bring it to your next session.

What's the question your brain keeps asking that nobody could actually answer?

[FEATURES: Turning why into what next || reflect | For the question you keep circling, a guided conversation that asks the follow-up questions, including what you could actually do next. || summaries | A weekly read of what took up your head, so the questions that repeat stop pretending to be new. || workspace | Park the one that will not let go, so it has somewhere to wait that is not your afternoon.]

Frequently asked questions

Why do I overthink everything?

People often overthink because the brain treats uncertainty as a problem to solve, and going over it again feels like progress. It can be a habit, a response to stress, or a way of trying to stay in control. If it's constant or distressing, a therapist can help you understand what's behind it in your case.

How do I stop overthinking a situation?

Change the kind of question you're asking. In a 2005 study, Watkins and Moulds found that concrete thinking about how things unfolded led to better problem solving than abstract thinking about why. From there, a practical next step is to ask what one thing you can do, set a point by which you'll decide, and say the loop out loud once so it exists outside your head.

What is the difference between overthinking and rumination?

Overthinking is the everyday word for going over something too much, while rumination is the psychological term for repetitive, passive thinking about your feelings, their causes and their consequences, without moving to action. Rumination usually looks back and asks why. Overthinking can also mean endless planning or second-guessing a decision you haven't made yet.

Is overthinking a sign of anxiety?

Overthinking often shows up alongside anxiety and low mood, but on its own it isn't a diagnosis. Almost everyone overthinks sometimes. If the worry doesn't let up, interferes with your sleep, work or relationships, or feels impossible to put down, that's a good reason to talk to a doctor or therapist rather than trying to diagnose yourself.

Does writing things down help with overthinking?

Writing your thoughts down, or saying them out loud, can help, because it turns a vague loop into something concrete you can look at. It helps most when it moves you toward a next step rather than another round of why. If writing only sends you over the same thoughts again, switch to a question about what you can do.
